content: Rosacea is a prevalent but often misunderstood skin condition that affects over 45 million individuals globally. It predominantly impacts fair-skinned individuals of northwestern European descent and is sometimes referred to as the curse of the Celts, particularly in Ireland. The condition typically begins with facial erythema, characterized by flushing and redness on the central face, including the cheeks, nose, and forehead. Less commonly, it may also affect the neck and chest. As rosacea progresses, additional symptoms may develop, such as persistent erythema, telangiectasia (visible dilation of superficial facial blood vessels), red papules (small bumps), pustules, gritty red eyes, burning or stinging sensations, and in severe cases, rhinophyma (a red, lobulated, and enlarged nose). Rosacea can be mistaken for or coexist with acne vulgaris or seborrheic dermatitis. While it affects both sexes, it is nearly three times more common in women and typically manifests between the ages of 30 and 60. The presence of a rash on the scalp or ears suggests an alternative or coexisting diagnosis, as rosacea primarily involves the face. There are four recognized subtypes of rosacea, and patients may exhibit more than one subtype simultaneously: 1. Erythematotelangiectatic Rosacea: This subtype is marked by permanent redness (erythema) with a tendency to flush or blush easily. Visible small blood vessels (telangiectasias) near the skin's surface are common, along with burning or itching sensations. 2. Papulopustular Rosacea: This subtype involves persistent redness accompanied by red bumps (papules) and pus-filled lesions (pustules) that typically last 1–4 days. It can be easily confused with acne. 3. Phymatous Rosacea: Most commonly associated with rhinophyma, this subtype involves thickened skin, irregular surface nodules, and tissue enlargement. It can also affect the chin (gnatophyma), forehead (metophyma), cheeks, eyelids (blepharophyma), and ears (otophyma). Telangiectasias may also be present. 4. Ocular Rosacea: This subtype presents with red, dry, and irritated eyes and eyelids. Symptoms may include a sensation of a foreign body, itching, and burning. Other descriptive terms have been applied to rosacea presentations, though they are not formally recognized as subtypes. These include granulomatous rosacea, rosacea fulminans (pyoderma faciale), perioral dermatitis (better described as periorificial dermatitis), persistent edema of rosacea, rosacea conglobata, and Morbihan disease (persistent redness and swelling of the upper face). Rosacea sufferers often report periods of depression due to cosmetic disfigurement, painful burning sensations, and a reduced quality of life. Causes Recent research by Richard L. Gallo and colleagues has identified elevated levels of the peptide cathelicidin and stratum corneum tryptic enzymes (SCTEs) in rosacea patients. Antibiotics, historically used to treat rosacea, may work by inhibiting SCTEs rather than through their antimicrobial properties. Rosacea has a hereditary component, with a higher genetic predisposition in fair-skinned individuals of European or Celtic ancestry. Women are more commonly affected, but men tend to experience more severe cases. While rosacea can occur at any age, it is most prevalent in individuals aged 30–50. Early signs include persistent redness triggered by exercise, temperature changes, or cleansing. Triggers that exacerbate flushing and blushing episodes contribute to the development of rosacea. These include exposure to temperature extremes, strenuous exercise, sunlight, severe sunburn, stress, anxiety, cold wind, and transitioning from cold to warm environments (e.g., entering heated buildings during winter). Certain foods and beverages, such as alcohol, caffeine-containing drinks (e.g., hot tea and coffee), histamine-rich foods, spicy foods, and antioxidant-rich fruits like red grapes, can also act as triggers. Some medications and topical irritants may worsen rosacea, and treatments like microdermabrasion, chemical peels, high doses of isotretinoin, benzoyl peroxide, and tretinoin have been reported to induce or exacerbate the condition. Steroid-induced rosacea can result from the use of topical or nasal steroids, often prescribed for seborrheic dermatitis. Gradual tapering of steroid use is recommended to avoid flare-ups. Studies have shown that some individuals with rosacea have increased numbers of Demodex mites, particularly in cases of steroid-induced rosacea. These mites may play a role in conjunction with other triggers. In some instances, Demodicidosis (mange) may mimic rosacea-like symptoms. Additionally, it has been suggested that rosacea may be a neurological disorder resulting from sensory neuron hypersensitization, potentially triggered by the activation of the plasma kallikrein-kinin system due to intestinal bacteria exposure. Treatments Treatment for rosacea varies based on severity and subtype. Dermatologists are advised to adopt a subtype-directed approach. While avoiding triggers can help reduce flare-ups, it is usually insufficient to achieve remission in all but mild cases. The National Rosacea Society recommends keeping a diary to identify and minimize triggers. A gentle skincare regimen using non-irritating cleansers is essential, along with daily sun protection using sunscreen with at least SPF 15 containing physical blockers like zinc oxide or titanium dioxide. Non-irritating chemical sunscreens are also an option. First-line treatments often include oral tetracycline antibiotics (e.g., tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline) and topical antibiotics like metronidazole to alleviate papules, pustules, inflammation, and some redness. Topical azelaic acid (e.g., Finacea) may help reduce inflammation. Oral antibiotics may also relieve ocular rosacea symptoms. For persistent papules and pustules, low-dose isotretinoin may be prescribed, though it is typically reserved for severe acne due to its side effects. Flushing and blushing have been treated with centrally acting α-2 agonists like clonidine, but there is no evidence of their efficacy. Similarly, beta-blockers like nadolol and propranolol have shown no benefit. Avoidance of red wine can help if it triggers flushing. Antihistamines have no proven benefit in rosacea treatment. For eyelid infections, frequent eyelid hygiene is crucial. This includes daily gentle scrubbing with diluted baby shampoo or over-the-counter eyelid cleansers and applying warm compresses several times a day. Dermatological vascular lasers (single wavelength) or intense pulsed light (broad spectrum) devices are among the most effective treatments for facial erythema. These devices target capillaries in the dermis, heating them to approximately 70°C, causing damage and subsequent absorption by the body’s natural defense mechanisms. CO2 lasers can be used to remove excess tissue caused by phymatous rosacea. Low-level light therapies have also been employed. Sulfur, once a popular treatment in the Victorian and Edwardian eras, has regained credibility as a safe alternative to steroids and coal tar for rosacea management.
